sum: Федеральное управление финансового надзора Германии BaFin 11 ноября 2026 года наложило административные штрафы на общую сумму 8 миллионов евро на Deutsche Bank из-за недостатков в миграции клиентов Postbank на общую ИТ-платформу банка. Уведомление регулятора BaFin было опубликовано 12 ноября.

Выводы касаются миграции данных клиентов Deutsche Bank в 2023 году в рамках проекта Unity. В BaFin заявили, что банк не создал адекватных организационных механизмов для оперативной обработки возросшего объема жалоб клиентов.

Второе нарушение касалось распоряжений о переводе счетов ценных бумаг. Регулятор заявил, что Deutsche Bank не выполнил заказы клиентов без промедления. Согласно действующим правилам, такие переводы должны быть осуществлены незамедлительно и не позднее трех недель.

Общая сумма в 8 миллионов евро включает 5,5 миллионов евро за медленную обработку жалоб и 2,5 миллиона евро за задержки переводов на счета ценных бумаг. Таким образом, дело касается организации и оказания инвестиционных услуг, а не изменения прогноза доходов банка.

В Deutsche Bank заявили, что с тех пор затронутые процессы улучшились. Для инвесторов штраф добавляет новую регулятивную проблему к истории интеграции Postbank, хотя финансовая сумма остается небольшой по сравнению с масштабом крупного европейского банка. Более важный вопрос заключается в том, предотвратит ли исправление дальнейшие расходы на обслуживание клиентов или соблюдение требований.

sum: This post may contain links from our sponsors and affiliates, and Flywheel Publishing may receive compensation for actions taken through them.

Elon Musk wrote on Sunday that SpaceX revenue “will drop” if computing power becomes plentiful and cheap, and on Tuesday Deutsche Bank raised its 2028 forecast for the company by $18 billion on the view that it will stay scarce. For a retiree who bought 1,000 shares of Space Exploration Technologies Corp. (NASDAQ: SPCX) on its first day of trading, the two statements land on the same $143,090 position.

Musk’s post on X, on the evening of Nov. 8, answered a clip of investor Chamath Palihapitiya arguing that SpaceX could cancel its Anthropic compute contract on 90 days’ notice and re-sign it at double the price. “It works both ways, of course,” Musk wrote. “If compute becomes plentiful and cheap, SpaceX revenue will drop. No crying in the casino for either party.”

Two days later, Deutsche Bank analyst Edison Yu told clients the casino is tilting SpaceX’s way. Voters backed limits on data-center development in 40 of 41 local ballot contests last week, by Ballotpedia’s count, and Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa has pledged to halt new approvals until the legislature sets protections for electricity costs and water. Yu expects that pressure to slow construction, mainly in 2028, which keeps computing capacity scarce and rental prices higher for longer. He raised his 2028 EBITDA forecast for SpaceX by $18 billion to $237.1 billion and his revenue forecast by $18.7 billion to $315.3 billion, and kept a Buy rating and a $250 price target.

Raising a 2028 forecast by $18 billion because of a construction slowdown reads as a bet that compute stays scarce for two more years and SpaceX gets to name its price; the limit of that reading is that Deutsche Bank left the contract repricing out of its numbers, and Musk himself says the price cuts both ways. The bank also notes that SpaceX’s own $24 billion gas plant and computing site in Texas faces the same approval freeze that would help its existing capacity.

Deutsche Bank's Record Quarter Meets a Lighter 2027 Capital Load
sum: Deutsche Bank shares climbed 4.0% yesterday, carried higher by a European banking sector that found its footing on a mix of dealmaking and strong results from peers. Reuters attributed the sector-wide strength to UniCredit's robust quarterly figures and the proposed combination involving Banco BPM and Crédit Agricole's Italian unit. The Euro Stoxx Banks index rose 3.1% on the day, with a pullback in oil prices further lifting the mood across financial stocks.
That sector tailwind is welcome, but it only tells part of the story. For Deutsche Bank, the more substantive developments are its own.

Roughly two weeks ago, the lender reported third-quarter 2026 results that included a record net profit of EUR 1.9 billion and a pre-tax profit of EUR 2.6 billion. Management also reaffirmed its full-year revenue target of more than EUR 33 billion. Those figures give the upbeat market sentiment a company-specific anchor — and a concrete starting point against which investors can measure future progress.

The distinction matters. Takeover speculation and rival earnings can shine a spotlight on an entire sector, but the quality of the case for any single bank rests on its own earnings power and its own regulatory requirements. In a broad upward move, expectations should track business performance rather than momentum.

On 27 October, Deutsche Bank disclosed that the ECB had set its Pillar 2 requirement for 2027 at 2.60% — a reduction of 25 basis points. The Pillar 2 requirement for the leverage ratio, according to the company, stays at 10 basis points.

That decision carries more weight than the general market mood because it speaks directly to the institution's regulatory obligations. A lower requirement is a positive factor for the bank; how much it ultimately benefits shareholders depends on how capital position and business develop from here. The relief applies to a specifically identified slice of the regulatory stack, and that nuance belongs in any sound assessment. The favorable guideline supports the company provided it simultaneously preserves its financial strength — which is why the combination of earnings growth and regulatory relief forms the strongest argument for a constructive stance on the stock.

sum: Siemens shares shed 2.9% on Friday as a global retreat from artificial intelligence and semiconductor names swept through the German market, with the industrial group caught up in a selloff that had no company-specific trigger.

Coverage of the session pointed to a hefty pullback on Wall Street and doubts over whether the returns on AI spending justify the sums being committed. One report also cited worries about tighter AI regulation as a factor weighing on sentiment in Frankfurt, where Siemens was named among the industrial stocks feeling the heat.

Deutsche Bank Research left its rating on Siemens at "Hold" with a price target of 270 euros on Friday. Analyst Gael de-Bray flagged mixed business signals from rivals in the automation arena, while pointing to a still-robust order trend in electrification as a counterweight for the Munich-based group.

The stock's slide did nothing to slow the pace of news from Siemens Mobility. On Friday the unit opened a new rail infrastructure technology and innovation centre in Chippenham, an investment of 115 million euros that the company says safeguards 800 local jobs.

A day earlier, Siemens Mobility disclosed orders from ST Engineering covering signalling work on Taiwan's Taoyuan Brown Line and the Green Line extension. The projects, to be equipped with the company's Signaling X technology, envisage fully automated operation among other features, with commissioning slated for the mid-2030s.

Midweek brought the closing of Siemens Mobility's acquisition of key core businesses from the MERMEC Group, completed on Wednesday once all required approvals were in hand. MERMEC was the seller of the acquired operations.

Siemens Mobility and Lufthansa Technik Defense signed a letter of intent on Tuesday to develop a rail-based patient transport train together. The unit is intended for military evacuations and civilian disaster relief, with capacity to care for more than 150 patients.

sum: Deutsche Bank shares shed 3.5% on Friday, caught in a broad European equity selloff that Reuters linked to waning risk appetite over AI-related stocks and US interest rates. The DAX also slipped as selling spread across the continent, with Germany's largest lender among the day's casualties. Nothing in the retreat was company-specific — but it sharpened the question investors now face: can earnings momentum carry the stock if the market backdrop stays hostile?

Goldman Sachs thinks the answer leans yes, with caveats. On Tuesday, following the quarterly report, analyst Chris Hallam raised his price target to EUR 47.75 from EUR 44.25 while keeping a "Buy" rating. His reasoning cut both ways: revenues came in above expectations, but so did costs. That single observation frames the debate — optimism about the top line is only worth as much as what survives on the bottom line.

Roughly two weeks ago, Deutsche Bank reported a record post-tax profit of EUR 1.9 billion for the third quarter of 2026, alongside a pre-tax result of EUR 2.6 billion. On the analyst call, management lifted its full-year 2026 revenue outlook to more than EUR 33 billion. The distinction matters: the profit figure describes a quarter already closed, while the revenue target is a forecast for the year ahead — an upgrade that went beyond the headline numbers.

That EUR 33 billion mark is now the key operational yardstick. It only earns the bank a better valuation if the extra income actually reaches the bottom line despite higher expenses. Revenue alone answers that question only in part, which is why Hallam's note directs attention to both sides of the profit equation. Investors would do well to read any future revenue commentary alongside cost trends.

Beyond the numbers, the bank confirmed on Thursday that it has launched an AI academy for more than 20,000 employees in its private bank division, with access being phased in gradually. For Germany, the rollout is scheduled for the first half of 2027 — the intended domestic start of an offering the bank has already flagged for the private bank as a whole.
Regulatory relief is also on the way. The ECB has set the Pillar 2 requirement at 2.60% from January 1, 2027 — 25 basis points below the current level.

Deutsche Bank's 2027 Question: Can Record Earnings Survive a Tougher Funding Climate?
sum: Deutsche Bank investors are being forced to weigh two competing narratives, and the tension between them has little to do with any single trading session. On one side sits the most profitable quarter the bank has ever posted. On the other, a gathering set of worries about what happens once the current cycle turns — specifically, whether the improved earnings power holds up through 2027.

The stock has been caught in the crossfire. It fell 3.5% in one session and 2.9% in another, both moves set against a broad selloff in European equities. The second decline came amid a global AI-driven retreat, with Reuters reporting concerns over potential restrictions on AI data centers, stretched valuations and debt-financed investment. Against that tape, company-specific progress struggles to register.

Roughly a week ago, Deutsche Bank lifted its full-year 2026 revenue guidance to more than EUR 33 billion. The cost target stayed put at around EUR 21.3 billion. That pairing is the real test: higher revenue has to materialize without the expense line creeping up to meet it. Judging the top line in isolation would miss the second half of the equation entirely.

The third-quarter report offers a starting point. Pre-tax profit for Q3 2026 rose 8% to EUR 2.6 billion, and net profit hit a record EUR 1.9 billion. Those figures, released about two weeks ago, underpin confidence in the bank's earning power — provided it can build on them.

Analysts currently expect earnings per share of EUR 3.31 for 2026, a concrete anchor for valuation. A dividend of EUR 1.16 per share is forecast for 2026, up from EUR 1.00 for 2025. That payout only strengthens the investment case if profits can carry it.

Goldman Sachs added its voice on Tuesday. According to media reports, the firm raised its price target to EUR 47.75 from EUR 44.25 while reaffirming its buy rating. Analyst Chris Hallam adjusted his estimates to reflect the quarterly report and described an "era of higher profitability." The stock also earned a place on Goldman's European list of particularly convincing investment ideas.
The direction of the estimate revision matters more than the target itself.

sum: Deutsche Bank upgraded JetBlue Airways to Buy from Hold on Thursday and lifted its price target to $5.50 from $3, citing a more favorable airline backdrop and planned product launches. The new target implies 54% upside to Wednesday’s close.

Deutsche Bank analyst Michael Linenberg said an industry focus on “yield in response to inflationary pressures,” including higher fuel prices, may disproportionately benefit airlines serving value-conscious, discretionary travelers. He also expects planned product launches at JetBlue and Frontier to support revenue and margins from 2027 onward.
The bank also cited positive airline returns in 21 of the last 25 years’ December quarters. The upgrade differed from the broader analyst view: 13 of 18 analysts covering JetBlue had Hold ratings.

JetBlue shares had gained more than 16% over the week through Thursday, following the airline’s Oct. 26 increase to its full-year revenue per available seat mile guidance. The stock remained down about 22% year to date as higher fuel costs tied to the Iran war pressured margins. JetBlue’s third-quarter results included a $257 million loss as its fuel bill rose 61%.

Recent trading has turned sharply positive for Deutsche Bank, with a 1-day share price return of 6.88% and a 7-day share price gain of 8.44% lifting the stock to €32.555. This comes even though the 90-day share price return is slightly down 0.52% and the year-to-date share price return is down 2.99%, while total shareholder return sits at 6.68% over 1 year. Deutsche Bank stock awaits London IPO revival after Numis deal
sum: Deutsche Bank's London investment-banking strategy is still waiting for a revival in initial public offerings, according to a Bloomberg report published on Wednesday, November 4, 2026. The report examines the progress of the bank's UK corporate-broker business three years after the Numis acquisition.

Deutsche Bank bought London-based corporate broker Numis in spring 2023, when market conditions appeared to be improving. The bank expected access to more than 160 Numis clients and hoped to win additional mandates from companies seeking listings on the London Stock Exchange.

That anticipated flow of transactions has not materialized. Bloomberg reports that initial public offerings have remained few and far between, leaving the strategic payoff from the acquisition dependent on a broader recovery in London's equity-capital-markets activity.

With the IPO market still subdued, Deutsche Bank has focused more heavily on larger British corporates. The lender is also seeking to sell additional banking services to existing Numis clients, broadening the commercial relationship beyond the original corporate-broker mandate.

The development matters for investors because the Numis deal was intended to strengthen Deutsche Bank's access to UK companies and potential capital-markets business. A prolonged shortage of listings limits the most visible source of growth, while the broader corporate approach may offer another route to building revenue from the acquired client base.

Volkswagen Keeps Deutsche Bank's Buy Rating Despite Trimmed Target as China Slide and Porsche Writed
sum: Deutsche Bank has trimmed its price target on Volkswagen's preference shares from EUR 105 to EUR 100 while leaving its buy recommendation in place, a two-speed signal that separates the bank from JPMorgan's more guarded stance on the embattled automaker.

Analyst Tim Rokossa cut the target following a sit-down with VW finance chief Arno Antlitz, an exchange he described as constructive. Talks centered on the ongoing restructuring, cost reduction in Germany and the worsening situation in China. The lower target nonetheless shows that even a positive read on management's plans was not enough to justify an unchanged valuation. The stock added 0.6% in the prior session.

JPMorgan had already moved on Friday, slashing its target from EUR 110 to EUR 85 after the quarterly figures while reaffirming a neutral rating. Media reports pointed to heavy one-off and write-down effects in the most recent quarter as the trigger. Both houses are marking down their valuation expectations; they part ways on what investors should do about it. A reduced target does not amount to a sell call — Deutsche Bank's underlying view stays positive, whereas JPMorgan remains on the sidelines.

The weaker earnings base explains the caution. Volkswagen booked a net loss after tax of EUR 5.8 billion for the third quarter of 2026, dragged down in large part by a non-cash Porsche goodwill impairment of EUR 6.4 billion. That figure cannot be read simply as a verdict on day-to-day operations — but neither does the write-down excuse the operating problems. Earnings power at the core Volkswagen brand remains the key test of the overhaul.

For the first nine months of 2026, the group reported operating profit of EUR 71 million, down from EUR 5,408 million a year earlier. Before special items, operating profit reached EUR 8.8 billion. Management stressed the immediate need for action in light of the nine-month balance sheet. For the full year, Volkswagen expects revenue of around EUR 315 billion and an operating return on sales of up to 1%.
At the brand level, Volkswagen Pkw generated operating profit of EUR 813 million from January to September 2026, a 1.3% operating margin that leaves limited financial headroom.

sum: A Deutsche Bank upgrade and a major AI infrastructure deal handed CrowdStrike two reasons to rally, yet the stock still fell. What that tells investors about the broader cybersecurity selloff is worth a closer look.

Two bullish headlines couldn’t keep CrowdStrike Holdings (NASDAQ:CRWD | CRWD Price Prediction) from slipping as cybersecurity stocks sold off to open the week. CrowdStrike stock is at $242.58, down 3% early in the session. Early gains tied to the upgrade news faded once the opening bell rang, extending a decline from the prior session.

Expectations were already elevated for CrowdStrike before the latest news arrived. Shares of the company are up 107% year to date (YTD), and a run that large can invite profit taking even on good news. Rotation within tech has picked up after a rough stretch for AI-linked stocks and heavy scrutiny of AI spending, making sector rotation another possible force behind the selling.

Deutsche Bank analyst Brad Zelnick upgraded CrowdStrike to Buy from Hold on November 2 and raised his price target to $300 from $240. Zelnick argued that investors underappreciate how much AI could expand the cybersecurity market, citing a “tsunami of cyber demand materializing as the AI frontier advances.” In his view, CrowdStrike’s own estimate of a $565 billion total addressable market by 2034 could prove conservative.

On the same day, CrowdStrike expanded its partnership with CoreWeave (NASDAQ:CRWV), giving CoreWeave customers access to the Falcon platform and round-the-clock managed security. Chief Business Officer Daniel Bernard explained the logic for CrowdStrike simply: “Production AI is becoming mission-critical, and adversaries know it.” For CrowdStrike, the deal expands its reach into AI infrastructure, a market management has highlighted as a major growth opportunity.

Both announcements build on CrowdStrike’s strong August 26 earnings report. Revenue at CrowdStrike rose 25.8% year over year (YoY) to $1.47 billion in Q2 FY2027, while net new annual recurring revenue (ARR) jumped 51% to $332.8 million. CrowdStrike also disclosed that Falcon Flex ending ARR topped $2.29 billion, up 101%, and it raised its full-year guidance.

Aixtron's Upgrades Cut Both Ways as Chip Selloff Drowns Out a Doubling Order Book
sum: Aixtron spent the week proving that a strong order book and a rising share price are two very different things. The German deposition-equipment maker watched its stock slide as a global semiconductor selloff swept through European chip names, with the day's move put at -4.4% in the latest reading — deepening from the -3.8% recorded a session earlier — as disappointing quarterly reports and cautious guidance from Amazon and Intel dragged the whole technology complex lower.

The retreat had nothing to do with anything Aixtron itself reported. Both accounts attribute the weakness squarely to the sector backdrop, not to any fresh negative company disclosure. What makes the episode worth unpacking is the collision it sets up: company-specific signals are improving at precisely the moment investors are re-pricing sector risk.

Deutsche Bank Research upgraded the stock from "Hold" to "Buy" — while trimming its price target to EUR 42 from EUR 44. Analyst Michael Kuhn pointed to continued positive momentum in equipment for optoelectronic chips and an earlier-than-expected recovery in power semiconductors. A better rating paired with a lower target is an unusual combination, and it frames the debate neatly: the demand picture is brightening, but the number attached to it came down.

The DZ Bank moved the other way on valuation. Analyst Armin Kremser cut his fair value to EUR 37.50 from EUR 40.00 and kept a "Hold" rating, flagging the production ramp and supply-chain assurance as live risks. Jefferies, for its part, reaffirmed its Buy recommendation with a EUR 44 target; analyst Om Bakhda highlighted accelerating order momentum in equipment for silicon carbide and gallium nitride chips.

Read together, the three opinions mark out two separate checkpoints for investors — the strength of demand on one side, the ability to execute on the other. Optimism about new orders does not erase operational reservations, and no analyst note substitutes for future results.

The concrete anchor for the bullish case landed on Thursday: Aixtron reported third-quarter 2026 order intake of EUR 274.9 million, up 122% year on year. sum: Nvidia is trading at record highs Tuesday, pushing its market capitalization to within roughly $200 billion of a $6 trillion milestone no company has ever crossed — and doing so precisely as the US bond market sends a macro warning signal that has not been this loud in nearly a quarter century. Deutsche Bank's research team has issued a direct challenge to the current equity rally: bonds and stocks are pricing two irreconcilable worlds, and one of them will have to yield.

Shares of the Santa Clara, California-based chipmaker have gained approximately 28% in 2026, adding more than $1.2 trillion to Nvidia's market value along the way. The rally has been relentless enough that the company is now closing in on a threshold that would have seemed unimaginable even 18 months ago: the first $6 trillion market capitalization in the history of publicly traded companies. At that level, Nvidia would be worth more than Amazon, Meta Platforms, Tesla, and Netflix combined.

The company's ascent from $1 trillion in June 2023 to the current approximately $5.8 trillion has been the fastest wealth creation run in stock market history, driven by an AI infrastructure boom that shows no structural signs of abating. Nvidia's share of the S&P 500 index has grown accordingly — the chipmaker now represents approximately 7 to 8% of the index, meaning its performance is directly embedded in the retirement portfolios of millions of Americans who have never bought a single share of NVDA.

A key accelerant for the October 2026 rally was a $150 billion increase to Nvidia's share repurchase authorization, announced September 28 — the largest single buyback in US corporate history. With the new authorization, Nvidia's total remaining repurchase capacity stands at $235 billion. CEO Jensen Huang described the backdrop as a "once-in-a-generation platform shift to AI and accelerated computing" and said the company planned to double chip shipments in 2027 as data center construction accelerates.

The specific reason Nvidia can sustain the valuation its stock reflects is a structural economic advantage that goes well beyond chip performance. When a hyperscaler — Amazon, Google, Microsoft, Meta — builds an AI training cluster, it is not simply buying graphics processing units.

sum: - If you are wondering whether Deutsche Bank's current share price still offers value or if most of the opportunity is already priced in, this article walks through the key signals you need to know.

- The stock closed at €26.96, with the share price down 2.8% over the past week, up 0.8% over the last month, down 19.7% year to date and up 14.5% over the past year. The three and five year returns are described as very large.

- On Simply Wall St's valuation checks, Deutsche Bank has a value score of 5 out of 6. The next sections will unpack what that means across different valuation methods, before finishing with a framework that can help you look beyond any single metric.

The Excess Returns model looks at whether a company is expected to earn more on its equity than it costs to fund that equity. It compares the return generated on each euro of book value with the required return investors expect, then capitalises those differences into an intrinsic value per share.

For Deutsche Bank, the model uses a Book Value of €41.47 per share and a Stable EPS of €3.94 per share, based on weighted future Return on Equity estimates from 13 analysts. The average Return on Equity input is 9.94%. Against this, the Cost of Equity is set at €4.09 per share, which leads to an Excess Return of €0.16 per share in decline rather than surplus. The Stable Book Value assumed in the model is €39.58 per share, drawn from estimates by 8 analysts.

Combining these inputs, the Excess Returns approach produces an intrinsic value of €37.72 per share for Deutsche Bank. Compared with the recent share price of €26.96, this implies the stock trades at a 28.5% discount, which screens as undervalued on this method.

Over the next two decades, stints at the Investment Bank and the Corporate Bank (the transaction banking hub) helped him identify how the next generation of financial services would build on new customer services originating in the post-trade world such as custody, safekeeping and asset servicing – resilient, cycle-proof and touching every part of the bank.

In 2025, Trust and Agency Services also became part of that story, and Maley was asked to manage the unified Trust and Securities Services (TSS) platform. He meets me from the bank’s New York office to expand on how the function engages with issuers and investors around the world.

At one stage, the securities services and trust and agency functions were combined, but were then made distinct businesses during Deutsche Bank’s overall restructuring in 2019, and then brought back together again last year. Maley explains the rationale: “Whether you look at issuers or investors, they’re part of one value chain. It’s issuer services, or trust and agency services, for the primary creation of new securities, the securitisation of those products, depository receipts and listing of those assets, and then the secondary market story at which point the owner of the underlying assets needs investor services such as asset servicing, tax processing and implementing corporate actions.”
The integrated business has a notable feature: it operates on both the private and public sides of Deutsche Bank.

items.t: Software shorts at the highest since the GFC, Deutsche Bank says
sum: Investing.com -- Short bets against software stocks have climbed to their highest level since the global financial crisis, according to a new report from Deutsche Bank.

Analyst Parag Thatte said the sector's sharp drawdown has pushed software shares "25% below their 200-day moving average," a drop he noted was "worse than the selloffs during the 2022 unwind of Tech and the March 2020 lockdown panic."

Thatte wrote that the median short interest across software companies has now surged "to over 5%, the highest in 17 years," placing it in the 93rd percentile over the past two decades. During the GFC, short interest peaked above 9%.
Deutsche Bank explained that past major selloffs were typically followed by earnings deterioration within one to two quarters.
In 2022, software earnings growth fell to zero, while in 2008–09 and 2001–02 it "turned outright negative."

Thatte also pointed to the energy sector's 2014 decline as an instructive comparison, noting that the sector sold off by 25% and continued falling as earnings collapsed over the next 18 months, with short interest rising until early 2016.

For software today, the bank said a further sustained decline would likely require evidence of weakening earnings. Even though consensus expects growth to slow from 26% in the fourth quarter of 2025 to 12% by late 2026, Thatte noted that forecasts for 2026 have been rising.

items.t: Deutsche Bank's (ETR:DBK) Dividend Will Be Increased To €1.00
sum: Deutsche Bank Aktiengesellschaft (ETR:DBK) has announced that it will be increasing its periodic dividend on the 2nd of June to €1.00, which will be 47% higher than last year's comparable payment amount of €0.68. The payment will take the dividend yield to 2.1%, which is in line with the average for the industry.
Deutsche Bank's Dividend Forecasted To Be Well Covered By Earnings
We like to see a healthy dividend yield, but that is only helpful to us if the payment can continue.

Having distributed dividends for at least 10 years, Deutsche Bank has a long history of paying out a part of its earnings to shareholders. Past distributions do not necessarily guarantee future ones, but Deutsche Bank's payout ratio of 26% is a good sign as this means that earnings decently cover dividends.
The next 3 years are set to see EPS grow by 40.0%. Analysts forecast the future payout ratio could be 35% over the same time horizon, which is a number we think the company can maintain.

The company has a long dividend track record, but it doesn't look great with cuts in the past. The dividend has gone from an annual total of €0.75 in 2016 to the most recent total annual payment of €0.68. Dividend payments have shrunk at a rate of less than 1% per annum over this time frame. A company that decreases its dividend over time generally isn't what we are looking for.

With a relatively unstable dividend, it's even more important to see if earnings per share is growing. We are encouraged to see that Deutsche Bank has grown earnings per share at 116% per year over the past five years. Earnings per share is growing at a solid clip, and the payout ratio is low which we think is an ideal combination in a dividend stock as the company can quite easily raise the dividend in the future.

items.t: Deutsche Bank launches Wero for more simple and sovereign digital payments in Europe
sum: Clients of Deutsche Bank and Postbank will from now on be able to send money and shop online across Europe using the Wero app

Effective immediately, Deutsche Bank and Postbank are offering their clients the full range of functions of the new digital payment app Wero. Since the beginning of the week, clients of both banks have been able to send and receive money in real time to family and friends across Europe with Wero, as well as pay in participating online shops. Postbank clients, who have already been able to transfer money to personal contacts with Wero since November 2024, have now been given the e-commerce function.

“Following the successful launch at Postbank, we are very pleased to offer the full range of Wero’s functions at Deutsche Bank and Postbank,” said Dominik Hennen, Head of Personal Banking at Deutsche Bank. “Wero is a decisive step towards a unified European payment landscape. We offer our clients an innovative solution that simplifies private and e-commerce payments even across national borders.”

“For Wero’s success, it is crucial that people can easily use the European payment solution in their daily lives. As The Global Hausbank, we not only offer Wero to our private clients, but are also a partner for European merchants and fintechs. We help them seamlessly integrate Wero as a payment option and reach their clients in Germany and four other European countries,” explained Kilian Thalhammer, Head of Merchant Solutions at Deutsche Bank.

"The launch of Wero by Deutsche Bank in Germany is a strong signal for the reachability and market penetration in Germany. We are very pleased to see Wero now enabling fast, secure P2P money transfers for all Deutsche Bank and Postbank customers, as well as instant and seamless payments at merchants that already accept Wero across Germany. This marks an important step toward a truly European payment solution," added Martina Weimert, CEO of EPI Company.

Wero is a digital payment solution that has been operated by the European Payments Initiative (EPI) since July 2024. Behind the EPI is an association of 16 major European banks and payment service providers that enable their clients to make instant transfers without entering IBAN and BIC as well as in future retail transactions.

The Digital Euro: A New Era for the European Monetary System
sum: By James von Moltke, President & CFO of Deutsche Bank, Katharina Paust-Bokrezion, Head of Payments & Digital Policy, Deutsche Bank AG and Manuel Klein, Head of Market Management Payments and Digital Currencies, Deutsche Bank AG.
This article has also been published on Schmalenbach IMPULSE.

Europe stands at a crossroads in the evolution of money. The digital euro project, spearheaded by the European Central Bank (ECB), is more than a technical innovation – it is a strategic response to profound shifts in the global payments landscape. Since the project’s inception, the debate has matured: stablecoins, especially those denominated in US dollars, have rapidly gained ground, and the EU’s regulatory frameworks are evolving to keep pace. The digital euro is now at the heart of discussions about Europe’s monetary sovereignty, competitiveness, and the future of payments.

As the ECB prepares to decide on the next phase of the digital euro, it is crucial to take stock of recent developments and ensure that Europe’s approach is both ambitious and pragmatic. This op-ed explores the digital euro’s role in the broader context of global monetary competition, the rise of stablecoins, and the imperative for public-private collaboration. It concludes with key recommendations for policymakers and industry leaders.

The digital euro project is unfolding against a backdrop of heightened geopolitical tensions and rapidly evolving economic and technological challenges. Recent years have underscored the importance of resilience and preparedness in Europe’s critical infrastructures, including payments. As the global environment becomes more complex, the need for robust, future-proof solutions to safeguard Europe’s financial stability and strategic autonomy has become increasingly apparent.
The digital euro, euro-denominated stablecoins and tokenised deposits together form a strategic triad for the future of European money.
In this context, new forms of digital money are gaining traction. Stablecoins have recently attracted greater attention as part of a broader trend towards digital assets.

Deutsche Bank is going for cut-price revenue growth in the investment bank
sum: Deutsche Bank is having an investor day. CEO Christian Sewing says the German bank wants to be “the European alternative in global banking and the gateway to Europe for clients around the world”. There are some big plans.

In its investment banking division, Deutsche Bank wants to increase revenues at a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of more than 15% a year between now and 2028. In its fixed income sales and trading business, it wants to grow revenues at a CAGR of 3% over the same period.

As it pumps its revenues, Deutsche Bank might need to hire some new people. Today's investment bank-specific presentation, from head of the investment bank Fabrizio Campelli, talks about investing across "industrials, FIG, healthcare and tech," implying new bankers to cover these verticals. In fixed income sales and trading, Campelli says the bank wants to "close competitive gaps" in areas like US flow credit trading and US securitized products. In technology, Campelli says Deutsche's investment bank wants to "invest in tech talent and capability," which suggests hiring there, too.

As Deutsche Bank's investment bank expands, it may not be splashing around the sorts of guaranteed bonuses that it has been known for in the past. Today's presentation from Campelli explains that the bank wants costs to consume just 30% of marginal revenues in the investment bank between now and 2028. Across the investment bank as a whole, costs are expected to consume 58% of revenues this year. The aspiration is therefore for future revenues in the investment bank to come at half the cost of current ones.

How will this happen? It's all about a "scalable operating model," says Campelli. There will be "tech led innovative solutions." There will be, "AI-enabled front-to-back automation and end-to-end process re-design." Most tellingly, there will also be "100% AI enabled engineers."
It sounds very ambitious. Deutsche Bank's share price is currently down nearly 1.7% today.
